\begin{frontmatter}

\title{Siamese metric learning for generalised few-shot recognition of rare viruses in transmission electron microscopy images}

%% Single-anonymised review: author names are shown. Replace the placeholders.
\author[a]{S. M. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed\corref{cor1}}
\ead{smmahbubuddinahmed@gmail.com}
\cortext[cor1]{Corresponding author.}
\affiliation[a]{organization={Independent Researcher},

\begin{abstract}
\textbf{Background and Objective:} The public TEM virus dataset contains 22 virus classes, but its benchmark covers only the 14 most frequent. The eight rare viruses, with 5--25 training micrographs each, have not been studied as few-shot classes. We examined whether a Siamese metric-learning encoder can recognise these rare viruses without training on them.

\textbf{Methods:} A DenseNet201 encoder was trained with a supervised contrastive loss on the 14 base classes, and the rare classes were added at test time as class prototypes (generalised few-shot learning). The encoder was compared with a re-implemented benchmark classifier under identical, leakage-audited evaluation on the official split. All hyper-parameters were selected on validation, and differences were assessed with paired micrograph-level cluster bootstrap tests.

\textbf{Results:} On the 14 base classes, the encoder reached \SiamClosedAccMean\,\% accuracy (macro-sensitivity \SiamClosedSensMean, macro-specificity \SiamClosedSpecMean) versus \BOneClosedAccMean\,\% for the baseline, with no significant difference in accuracy for any seed pair. Confused rare classes were nearly linearly separable in the learned features. Replacing nearest-prototype classification with logistic regression on the frozen features raised the 22-class macro-F1 from \SiamGfslFOneMean\ to \SiamLrFOneMean, a significant gain for every checkpoint. With one example per rare virus, Siamese features gave higher rare-class accuracy than baseline features (\KshotSiamOneMean\,\% versus \KshotBOneOneMean\,\%), but this advantage disappeared with three or more examples.

\textbf{Conclusions:} Siamese metric learning matches a strong classifier on this benchmark and is advantageous in the one-shot setting. For rare viruses, most of the attainable improvement comes from the decision rule rather than the representation.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keyword}
transmission electron microscopy \sep virus classification \sep few-shot learning \sep metric learning \sep rare classes
\end{keyword}

\end{frontmatter}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Negative-stain transmission electron microscopy (TEM) can identify a virus without prior knowledge of what to look for, but interpreting the images requires scarce expertise. This has motivated automatic classification of virus particles in TEM images. Matuszewski and Sintorn released a public TEM virus dataset \cite{MS21,MS21data}: 1,245 micrographs of 22 viruses, patches at 1\,nm/pixel and an official, representative, micrograph-level train/validation/test split. Their benchmark uses the 14 most frequent classes, on which a fine-tuned DenseNet201 reached 93.1\,\% test accuracy. Eight classes were excluded because they had too few images or particles to train a classifier reliably.

Rare viruses are, however, the realistic diagnostic case: a newly emerging virus will always have few reference images. This is the setting of few-shot learning, and more precisely of generalised few-shot learning (GFSL), in which new classes must be recognised alongside the training classes \cite{GK18}. Siamese metric learning is well suited to this setting. A shared-weight encoder maps patches of the same virus close together, and a new virus is represented by the mean embedding (prototype) of its few examples, without retraining. Because the benefit of few-shot methods can be overestimated when they are compared with weak baselines (Section~\ref{sec:related}), a credible evaluation must compare them with a strong classification baseline under identical conditions.

To our knowledge no published work has applied metric-learning few-shot methods to this dataset or evaluated its rare classes as few-shot classes. Our contributions are:
(i) a GFSL protocol for all 22 classes on the official split, in which the rare classes are never used for training and every choice is made on validation;
(ii) a Siamese supervised-contrastive encoder compared with a faithful re-implementation of the benchmark classifier under identical evaluation;
(iii) a diagnosis showing that rare-class errors stem from the nearest-prototype decision rule rather than the representation, and an evaluation of classifiers on frozen features that addresses them; and
(iv) full reporting of negative results, with code, logs and per-patch predictions released.

\subsection{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\textbf{Virus classification on the TEM virus dataset.} The benchmark of Matuszewski and Sintorn \cite{MS21} compared a custom CNN with eight ImageNet-pretrained architectures on the 14-class split and also showed that an unrepresentative split lowers performance substantially, which makes the official split the reference protocol. Later 14-class studies proposed ensembles of CNNs and vision transformers \cite{N23}, p4-equivariant group convolutions that improve data efficiency \cite{BB24}, a compact dual-branch CNN fed with local-standard-deviation and discrete-cosine-transform images \cite{S24}, and a DenseNet-based dual-track network with attention \cite{B25}. These studies reported accuracies between 84.49\,\% and 99.73\,\%, but under different protocols. They used a different train--test ratio \cite{N23}, a reduced training set with results on the validation split \cite{BB24}, or a random split of the augmented patch set \cite{S24}, and one did not report its protocol in the accessible text \cite{B25}. Their accuracies are therefore not directly comparable with each other or with the official benchmark. Two studies used all 22 classes: a dilated multilevel fused CNN \cite{U24} and a CNN--transformer hybrid evaluated on a stratified split \cite{H26}, with accuracies of 89.89\,\% and 88.31\,\%, respectively. Both trained a closed-set classifier on every class. As far as we could determine, neither reported rare-class results on the official split or treated the rare viruses as few-shot classes.

\textbf{Siamese networks, metric learning and few-shot baselines.} Siamese networks learn a shared-weight encoder and compare inputs by distance \cite{Bro93,Koc15}. Prototypical networks extend this idea to $N$-way classification with class-mean prototypes \cite{Sne17}. Batch-based losses, namely the batch-hard triplet loss \cite{Sch15,Her17} and the supervised contrastive (SupCon) loss \cite{Kho20}, use every positive and negative pair in a class-balanced batch and train such encoders more efficiently than isolated pairs. Several studies have shown that a well-trained embedding with a simple classifier, such as nearest class mean after centring and normalisation \cite{Wan19} or logistic regression on frozen features \cite{Tia20}, rivals more elaborate meta-learning \cite{Che19}, and that the advantage of meta-learning shrinks under strong domain shift \cite{Guo20}. Richer decision rules on frozen features include class-specific Mahalanobis distances with shrunk covariances \cite{Bat20} and distribution calibration, which borrows feature statistics from related base classes \cite{Yan21}.

\textbf{Generalised few-shot learning and medical imaging.} In GFSL, new classes must be recognised among the training classes \cite{GK18}. The classification scores are typically biased towards the training classes, a bias that calibrated stacking counteracts \cite{Cha16}. In medical imaging, a systematic review of 80 few-shot studies found meta-learning to be the most common approach \cite{PC23}. Few-shot recognition of viruses in TEM images, in which the rare classes are held out from training and evaluated on an official split, has, to our knowledge, not been studied.

\section{Methods}
\label{sec:methods}

\subsection{Dataset and leakage control}
\label{sec:data}

We used the official patch folders of the dataset \cite{MS21data}: $256\times256$-pixel patches centred on annotated particles, after rescaling to 1\,nm/pixel. The split assigns whole micrographs to train, validation or test (about 60/20/20\,\%) \cite{MS21}. The 14 benchmark classes are the \emph{base} classes. The eight excluded classes, which the dataset provides in the same split, are the \emph{rare} classes (Table~\ref{tab:data} and Fig.~\ref{fig:dataset}). The pre-augmented, class-balanced training set (736 patches per base class) was used only to re-implement the benchmark classifier, as in the original work.

Each patch was standardised to zero mean and unit variance \cite{MS21} and its grey channel replicated to three channels. Patches were not resized. Before training we audited the data at pixel level: none of the 16,441 training and augmented-training patches is identical to any rotation or reflection of a validation or test patch, and no test patch matches a validation patch.

\subsection{Siamese metric-learning encoder}
\label{sec:siamese}

\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/architecture.pdf}
\caption{Overview of the method. (a) Training: patches of the 14 base classes pass through one DenseNet201 encoder with shared weights (drawn as parallel Siamese branches); a projection head maps the pooled feature $\bm{h}$ to a unit-norm embedding $\bm{z}$, and the supervised contrastive loss pulls together patches of the same virus and pushes apart patches of different viruses. (b) Inference: the head is discarded and the frozen encoder embeds the support patches of all 22 classes, including the eight rare classes never used for training, into class prototypes; a test patch is assigned by nearest class mean or by a classifier fitted on the frozen features, chosen on the validation split. Example patches are from the TEM virus dataset \cite{MS21data} (CC BY 4.0).}
\label{fig:arch}
\end{figure}

The encoder (Fig.~\ref{fig:arch}a) is an ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet201 \cite{Hua17,Den09}. Global average pooling yields a 1,920-dimensional \emph{backbone feature}, and a two-layer projection head (1,920$\to$512$\to$128 units) with L2 normalisation produces the embedding used by the loss. All patches pass through the same weights, so similarities are computed in a single shared space. The network was trained with the supervised contrastive loss \cite{Kho20}. Each batch contained several patches of every base class, and the patches of a class were drawn from different micrographs where possible. Augmentation used the eight exact rotations and reflections of the square and small translations, which preserve the physical scale. The network was optimised with AdamW \cite{LH19}; all training settings are listed in Table~\ref{tab:config}. The checkpoint with the highest validation macro-F1 of nearest-prototype classification over the base classes was retained, and training stopped early when this score no longer improved (Fig.~\ref{fig:training}). The rare classes were never seen during training or model selection.

Pilot experiments in which four base classes were withheld from training showed that the backbone feature transfers to unseen classes whereas the 128-dimensional head does not (\ref{app:pilots}). We therefore fixed the backbone feature as the representation for all experiments before evaluating the main models.

\subsection{Baselines}
\label{sec:baselines}

The \textbf{baseline} is a re-implementation of the best benchmark model \cite{MS21}, based on its published configuration and code. It consists of DenseNet201 followed by two fully connected layers with dropout and a softmax output over the 14 base classes. It was trained with cross-entropy on the pre-augmented training set, and the checkpoint with the highest validation accuracy was retained (Table~\ref{tab:config}). The baseline and the Siamese encoder were each trained with three seeds. The pooled DenseNet201 features of the baseline also serve as an alternative backbone in every few-shot experiment, which isolates the effect of the training objective. A \textbf{fully supervised reference}, a DenseNet201 with a linear head trained with class-balanced sampling on all 22 classes, sees the rare classes during training and is reported for comparison only. Two loss ablations were trained once: the batch-hard triplet loss \cite{Her17} and SupCon with an auxiliary cosine-classifier term \cite{Che19}.

\subsection{Evaluation protocols}
\label{sec:protocols}

All results are reported on the official test split. Each patch is represented by the mean over its eight rotations and reflections, computed with \InferenceMode\ inference. Three protocols were used. In the \emph{closed-set} protocol (14 classes), test patches are assigned to the nearest class mean by cosine similarity, with prototypes computed from all training patches. The baseline uses its own softmax output. In the \emph{GFSL} protocol (22 classes, Fig.~\ref{fig:arch}b), prototypes of all classes are computed from the training split, and the 2,057 test patches are classified among all 22 classes. In the \emph{K-shot GFSL} protocol, each rare class receives only $K\in\{1,3,5,10\}$ training patches from different micrographs, drawn at random \KshotDraws\ times, while the base classes keep all their training patches. We report accuracy, macro-F1, base-class accuracy and the rare-class mean per-class accuracy. The last measure is preferred to pooled accuracy because the rare-class test sets range from 7 to 44 patches. Results for episodes and unknown-virus detection are given in \ref{app:extra}.

\subsection{Classifiers on frozen features}
\label{sec:classifiers}

To test whether the rare-class errors stem from the representation or from the decision rule, four classifiers were fitted on the frozen backbone features of every checkpoint, without modifying the encoder. These were (i) the nearest class mean, (ii) L2-regularised logistic regression with class-balanced weights \cite{Tia20}, (iii) a Mahalanobis classifier whose class covariances are shrunk towards the pooled covariance in a 64--256-dimensional principal-component space, following Simple CNAPS \cite{Bat20}, and (iv) distribution calibration, which samples synthetic features for each rare class from the statistics of its nearest base classes \cite{Yan21}. Each classifier was fitted on the training split, and its hyper-parameters were chosen by the 22-class macro-F1 on the validation split. The chosen setting was then applied once to the test split. Before any test result was examined, we fixed the rule that the classifier with the highest validation macro-F1 is the one reported as the improvement. All four classifiers are nevertheless reported. In a separability diagnostic, a binary logistic regression was trained on the training patches of each of eight confusable pairs and evaluated on their validation patches.

\subsection{Statistics}
\label{sec:stats}

Confidence intervals (95\,\%) come from a stratified micrograph-level cluster bootstrap that resamples micrographs within classes \cite{ET93}. Paired comparisons on identical test patches use a paired cluster bootstrap of the difference in accuracy and macro-F1, together with an exact McNemar test \cite{McN47}. Because the McNemar test treats patches as independent, it is anti-conservative when patches share micrographs. The conclusions therefore rest on the cluster bootstrap. The Siamese encoder and the baseline are compared for all $3\times3$ seed pairs, and K-shot comparisons are paired over identical support draws. Values over seeds are given as mean $\pm$ standard deviation.

\subsection{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

Experiments used PyTorch 2.11 and scikit-learn on one NVIDIA RTX 3060 (12\,GB). The analysis code was written with the assistance of an AI tool (Claude, Anthropic) and was checked with 23 automated tests, including comparisons of the loss functions and evaluation metrics against independent reference implementations. Training took 19--28\,min per seed for the Siamese encoder and about 134\,min per seed for the baseline.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{14-class benchmark}

The Siamese encoder performed on par with the baseline (Table~\ref{tab:closed}). It was more accurate in all nine seed pairs, but none of the differences in accuracy was statistically significant, and only one pair differed significantly in macro-F1. Every seed of both models exceeded the published accuracy of 93.1\,\%. Because test-time augmentation and implementation details differ from the original study, the re-trained baseline rather than the published figure is the appropriate comparator. The 128-dimensional projection head scored slightly higher on the base classes (Table~\ref{tab:closed}). However, it was not the pre-specified representation, its advantage over the baseline was not significant in the seed-0 comparison, and it fails on unseen classes (Section~\ref{sec:res-gfsl}).

\subsection{22-class generalised few-shot recognition}
\label{sec:res-gfsl}

With nearest-prototype classification over all 22 classes, the Siamese and baseline features reached the same macro-F1 (Table~\ref{tab:gfsl}). The Siamese features were more accurate overall, mainly because they classified the base classes better, whereas the baseline features recognised the rare classes slightly better. The accuracy advantage of the Siamese features was significant in only two of the nine seed pairs. For seed 0, the patch-level McNemar test indicated a significant difference ($p=\CmpGfslMcP$) although the cluster bootstrap interval included zero, which illustrates why the conclusions rest on the cluster bootstrap. The 128-dimensional head collapsed on the rare classes, with a rare-class mean accuracy of only \HeadRareMin--\HeadRareMax\,\%. A large gap remained to the fully supervised reference, which had been trained on the rare classes. The errors were concentrated in a few rare viruses. In every seed, most Dengue test patches (\DengueToSapMin--\DengueToSapMax\ of \DengueTest) were assigned to Sapovirus.

\subsection{Rare classes are separable}

Every confusable pair was close to linearly separable in the learned features, with a validation AUROC of at least \SepAucMin\ (Table~\ref{tab:sep}). Nevertheless, the two-class nearest-mean rule performed far worse than a linear boundary for several pairs. For Sapovirus versus Astrovirus, it was close to chance, whereas logistic regression separated the pair well. The information needed to recognise the rare viruses is therefore present in the representation but is not exploited by an isotropic distance to the class mean. Because the rare-class validation sets are small (10--16 patches), these values should be regarded as indicative.

\subsection{Classifiers on frozen features}

The pre-declared selection rule chose logistic regression for six of the seven checkpoints, including all three Siamese seeds (Table~\ref{tab:clf}). The only exception was \LrWinExceptions. For the Siamese encoder, logistic regression raised the 22-class macro-F1 from \SiamNcmFOneMean\ to \SiamLrFOneMean\ and also improved the base-class accuracy. The gain over the nearest class mean was significant for all seven checkpoints. Among the weakest rare classes, the F1 score of Dengue rose from \WeakDengueNcm\ to \WeakDengueLr\ (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:weak}).

Fig.~\ref{fig:confusion} shows that the improvement came mainly from higher precision. Averaged over the eight rare classes, precision increased from \RarePrecNcm\ to \RarePrecLr, whereas recall changed less (from \RareRecNcm\ to \RareRecLr). With the nearest class mean, many patches of other classes were assigned to some rare classes. For example, the precision for Sapovirus was only \PrecSapoNcm. Dengue remained the most difficult class. Even with logistic regression, \DengueToSapPctLr\,\% of its test patches were assigned to Sapovirus, compared with \DengueToSapPctNcm\,\% with the nearest class mean. The shrunk Mahalanobis classifier reached a similar macro-F1, but its validation scores were almost identical across settings, so its test result depends on near-ties. We therefore report it as a secondary result.

With all rare-class training data available, the Siamese training objective gave no advantage, because logistic regression on the baseline features reached a similar macro-F1 (Table~\ref{tab:clf}). The difference between the two feature sets was significant in only one of the nine seed pairs, in favour of the baseline.

Classifiers that estimate more parameters required more data. With a single example per rare class, logistic regression reached a rare-class mean accuracy of only \SiamLrKOneMean\,\%, compared with \SiamNcmKOneMean\,\% for the nearest class mean (Table~\ref{tab:clf}). Distribution calibration, in contrast, improved on the nearest class mean in this setting, significantly for all six Siamese and baseline checkpoints. With distribution calibration, the Siamese and baseline features performed similarly.

\subsection{Few-shot regime}

With one training patch per rare virus, the Siamese features gave a higher rare-class mean accuracy than the baseline features, \KshotSiamOneMean\,\% versus \KshotBOneOneMean\,\% (Fig.~\ref{fig:kshot}). When paired over identical support draws, the difference was significant in all nine seed pairs. From three examples onwards, the baseline features performed equally well or better (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:kshot}).

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

Under an identical, leakage-audited protocol, a Siamese supervised-contrastive encoder with a nearest-prototype classifier performed on par with a re-implementation of the strongest published benchmark model on the 14 base classes. Its features also allow new virus classes to be added without retraining. In the most data-scarce setting, with a single reference patch per new virus classified by the nearest prototype, the Siamese encoder recognised rare viruses better than features learned with cross-entropy, consistently across all seed pairs. This is the setting that motivates few-shot learning for diagnostic TEM, because the first image of an emerging virus can be added as a prototype immediately.

The advantage did not persist with three or more examples, in rare-class-only episodes, when distribution calibration was used, or once a linear classifier was fitted on all available rare-class data. With nearest-prototype classification over all 22 classes, the two feature sets also reached the same macro-F1. These findings agree with previous reports that the quality of the embedding, rather than the metric-learning objective, dominates few-shot performance \cite{Che19,Tia20}. They also indicate that claims of superiority for metric-learning approaches on this dataset should be tested against an identically evaluated classification baseline.

The most practically relevant result concerns the rare classes, which previous 22-class studies did not analyse. Dengue, Sapovirus, Guanarito and LCM were poorly recognised by prototype classification, although they are nearly linearly separable from the classes with which they are confused. The distance to a class mean ignores differences in class spread, which is plausible for rare classes whose few micrographs differ in staining and particle density. A validation-selected logistic regression recovered much of the gap to the fully supervised reference (macro-F1 of \SiamLrFOneMean\ versus \CeFOne) without retraining the encoder. However, this classifier requires enough examples. With one to five examples per class, the nearest class mean or distribution calibration should be preferred.

Published 22-class results were obtained by training on all classes with different or unreported splits \cite{U24,H26}, so they are not directly comparable with ours. For reference, the fully supervised model trained on all classes with our pipeline reached \CeAcc\,\% accuracy on the official split.

\textbf{Limitations.} The rare classes have only 2--8 test micrographs each, so the per-class F1 scores of the smallest classes, such as Sapovirus and Guanarito with fewer than ten test patches each, are highly uncertain. The ablations were trained with a single seed. The hyper-parameters of the frozen-feature classifiers were chosen on small rare-class validation sets, which adds selection variance, as the Mahalanobis results show. Finally, we studied one backbone and one dataset, and the unknown-virus detection reported in \ref{app:extra} is not yet adequate for deployment.

%% ======================================================================
\section{Conclusions}

To our knowledge, this is the first generalised few-shot evaluation of all 22 classes of the public TEM virus dataset on its official split, with the rare classes never used for training. A Siamese metric-learning encoder performs on par with a strong re-implemented classifier on the benchmark. With nearest-prototype classification, it recognises rare viruses better when only one reference patch is available, but not when more examples are available. Most of the attainable improvement on rare viruses comes from replacing nearest-prototype classification with a validation-selected linear classifier on frozen features, for either training objective. The protocol, code and per-patch predictions are released for future comparisons.

\appendix

\section{Pilot experiments}
\label{app:pilots}

Four base classes were withheld from encoder training (F2: Astrovirus, Influenza, Papilloma, Rotavirus; F3: Marburg, Orf, Adenovirus, CCHF) and used as unseen classes, with micrograph-disjoint episodes (600 episodes, 15 queries per class). Without training, ImageNet features reached only \PilotFrozenNcm\,\% nearest-mean accuracy on the 14 classes (\PilotFrozenProbe\,\% with a linear probe). After training, the backbone feature transferred to the unseen classes, whereas the 128-dimensional head did not; in the F3 GFSL test head accuracy on the unseen classes was \PilotHeadUnseen\,\% (Table~\ref{tab:pilots}).

The training curves of the three Siamese and three baseline runs are shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:training}. The Siamese runs stopped early once the validation macro-F1 had not improved for 12 epochs. The baseline was trained for the fixed 50 epochs of the original configuration. Its validation accuracy fluctuated from epoch to epoch, so the selected checkpoint (highest validation accuracy) varies between seeds.
